standard.title: Different Experiences and Perspectives of Colonisers and First Nations Australians
standard.description: different experiences and perspectives of colonisers, settlers and First Nations Australians and the impact of these experiences on changes to Australian society's ideas, beliefs and values
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the founding contexts of colonies (AC9HH9K02), the effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians (AC9HH9K03), and the development of Australian society toward Federation (AC9HH9K04–K05). They have a grounding in the different conditions experienced by different groups in colonial Australia. This descriptor asks them to explicitly compare perspectives and assess impact on ideas, beliefs and values — moving from description of events to analysis of meaning and experience.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate different experiences and perspectives of colonisers, settlers and First Nations Australians and explain the impact of these experiences on changes to Australian society's ideas, beliefs and values.

nodes.label: Experiences of convicts and free settlers
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the experiences of specific arrival groups in colonial Australia and explain how colonial conditions enabled or constrained new identities and social mobility.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the experiences of one colonial arrival group (convicts or free settlers) and explain one way their experiences influenced Australian social values or identity.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the experiences of convicts in specific colonies; examine how convict transportation enabled social mobility away from rigid British class structures; examine how free settlers experienced a different set of colonial conditions; compare how these different experiences contributed to emerging Australian values (egalitarianism, 'fair go', anti-authoritarianism).
wider: Examine specific notable convict figures (e.g. Francis Greenway, Samuel Terry) and assess how their contributions complicate simple narratives of convict life — examining the range of outcomes from convict transportation

Investigate how class structures changed (or failed to change) in colonial Australia — examining whether the 'egalitarian' colonial myth reflected reality for all groups, including women, First Nations Australians, and non-European migrants

response_modes.reason: Using both convict and free settler experiences, and examining how each group's conditions shaped different relationships to Australian identity, is more valuable than depth on one group only.

success_criteria: Describes the experiences of at least one colonial arrival group with specific historical detail
Explains how colonial conditions shaped at least one aspect of emerging Australian social values or identity

nodes.label: Non-European experiences in colonial Australia
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the experiences of non-European groups in Australia prior to the 1900s and explain how their treatment shaped emerging Australian attitudes toward race and citizenship.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the experiences of one non-European group in colonial Australia and explain one way their treatment influenced Australian social attitudes.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the experiences of non-European groups including Chinese migrants on the goldfields in Victoria and New South Wales, Japanese pearlers in northern Australia, South Sea Islanders on Queensland sugar plantations, and Afghan cameleers in central Australia; explain how the treatment of these groups — including racial discrimination, exclusion, and deportation — reflected and reinforced the racial ideology that would be codified in the Immigration Restriction Act 1901.
wider: Investigate the experiences of Chinese miners on the Victorian goldfields in depth — examining the conditions of discrimination, violence, and exclusion they faced and the communities they built despite this

Examine the South Sea Islander (Kanaka) labour experience on Queensland sugar plantations — including questions about consent, coercion, and the 'blackbirding' practice — to assess the degree to which this labour was effectively enslaved

Trace how the treatment of non-European groups in colonial Australia fed directly into the 'White Australia Policy' at Federation — examining the connection between colonial racial practice and federal racial legislation

response_modes.reason: Multiple non-European groups experienced colonial Australia differently — examining at least two prevents students from generalising and shows how racial hierarchy operated across different contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The experiences of non-European groups in colonial Australia are both historically significant and relatively underrepresented in mainstream historical narratives — there is rich material here for examining how race was constructed, contested, and institutionalised in Australian history.
success_criteria: Examines the experiences of at least one non-European group in colonial Australia with specific historical detail
Explains how the treatment of non-European groups influenced Australian attitudes toward race and citizenship

nodes.label: First Nations perspectives and contested historical language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore the perspectives and experiences of First Nations Australians and discuss why terms such as 'invasion', 'colonisation' and 'settlement' remain contested.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain why the terms 'invasion', 'colonisation' and 'settlement' are used differently to describe the same historical events, and identify whose perspective each term reflects.
nodes.typical_width: Explore First Nations Australian perspectives on colonisation; discuss why terms like 'invasion', 'colonisation' and 'settlement' remain contested within Australian society today; explain how the choice of language reflects the perspective of the speaker and carries different implications for understanding historical responsibility and present-day relationships.
wider: Examine primary and secondary sources using both 'settlement' and 'invasion' framings of the same events and analyse what each framing reveals and obscures — developing students' capacity to read language as a historical and political choice
Investigate how the language used in Australian history textbooks has changed over time, examining when and why 'settlement' began to be qualified or replaced by 'invasion' in some historical writing
Explore contemporary First Nations perspectives on the language debate through speeches, writing, or media — examining how this is not only a historical question but a live political and cultural one

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the full Australian colonial history strand — asking students to reflect on how language, perspective, and historical framing shape our understanding of the entire period studied. It is the point at which historical thinking becomes explicitly meta-historical.

success_criteria: Explains why the terms 'invasion', 'colonisation' and 'settlement' carry different meanings and whose perspectives they represent
Discusses at least one way this language debate connects to present-day Australian society
